title: 2025 Federal Agency AI Use Case Inventory (consolidated)
measure: AI use cases publicly reported by US civilian federal agencies (count), and those classed rights-/safety-impacting (2024) or high-impact (2025)
latest_value: 3,611 use cases; 445 high-impact; 56 agency submissions (as of 13 Apr 2026)
finding: Disclosed use cases rose from 710 (2023) to 2,133 (2024, final) to 3,611 (2025), while reporting rules widened and the impact category was redefined.
limits: counts paperwork, not decisions; Defense and intelligence excluded; rule changes each year; 2023 figure via press

cite: US OMB 2026 (observatory tabulation of the use-case CSV)
title: 2025 inventory: minimum-practice fields for high-impact AI use cases
measure: Of high-impact use cases recorded as deployed, the number reporting each minimum practice (appeal process, pre-deployment testing, impact assessment, ongoing monitoring) as established
latest_value: Of 227 deployed high-impact uses: appeal process established 16 (7%); testing done 44 (19%); impact assessment done 36 (16%); monitoring established 40 (18%); about 101 blank (submissions due 22 Dec 2025)
finding: Of 227 deployed high-impact federal AI uses, only 16 (7%) report an established appeal route and 44 (19%) completed testing; most of the rest say 'in progress' or leave the field blank.
limits: agency self-report; filed before M-25-21's April 2026 compliance deadline; many blanks; 2024 fields not comparable (22 of 154 operating rights/safety-impacting uses reported an appeal process in the 2024 first release)

title: 2024 inventory field 57: can the AI make individual high-impact decisions without direct human involvement?
measure: Use cases where the agency answered that all individual decisions are automated, versus some requiring direct human oversight (count)
latest_value: 3 'Yes – all individual decisions automated'; 143 'No – some require direct human oversight'; 3 human intervention impracticable with fail-safe; 1,554 blank (first release, 1,757 use cases)
finding: In the only federal inventory that asked, agencies said 3 use cases make all individual decisions without direct human involvement; the 2025 form dropped the question.
limits: one round; mostly blank; first-release file (1,757 of the final 2,133); question removed in 2025

title: 2025 inventory: vendors named for AI use cases
measure: Use cases whose free-text vendor field names each company (count and share of those naming a vendor)
latest_value: Vendor named for 790 of 3,611 uses; Microsoft in 133 (17%). Of 311 generative-AI uses naming a vendor: Microsoft 100, OpenAI 34, Google 21, Amazon/AWS 18, Palantir 15, Anthropic 6
finding: Where agencies name a supplier, Microsoft dominates: it appears in 100 of the 311 generative-AI use cases that name one (32%).
limits: free-text field, blank for 78% of uses; keyword matching by the observatory; Azure OpenAI counts towards both Microsoft and OpenAI; one reading

title: 2025 inventory: development stage and topic of AI use cases
measure: Use cases by development stage and topic area (count, share of 3,611)
latest_value: Deployed 1,040 (29%); pilot 440; pre-deployment 1,479 (41%); retired 314; science, admin or IT 1,582 (44%); benefits processing 56; law enforcement 285; deployed and high-impact 227 (6%)
finding: Most disclosed federal AI is not yet deployed or is back-office: 29% deployed, 44% in science, admin or IT, and 227 (6%) both deployed and high-impact.
limits: stage blank for 338 and topic blank for 603; OMB's summary counts 1,818 'deployed and piloted', more than the CSV stage field gives (1,480); categories changed from 2024

title: Artificial Intelligence: Generative AI Use and Management at Federal Agencies (GAO-25-107653)
measure: AI and generative-AI use cases in the inventories of 11 selected agencies, 2023 vs 2024 (count)
latest_value: 1,110 AI and 282 generative-AI use cases (2024), up from 571 and 32 (2023)
finding: At 11 agencies, generative-AI use cases rose about ninefold in a year (32 to 282) while all AI use cases nearly doubled; 10 of 12 agencies reported difficulty complying with federal AI policy.
limits: inventory rules widened in 2024; 61% of 2024 generative-AI uses were mission-enabling (internal)

title: GAO-26-107859 on federal AI acquisitions (as reported by ExecutiveGov, 14 Apr 2026)
measure: Agencies' practices and challenges in buying AI
finding: Agencies lack technical experts to judge vendors' AI, struggle to understand AI costs, and do not systematically share lessons; GSA, the Department of War, DHS and VA policies bar collecting them.
limits: read via trade press, not GAO's page; no figures

title: Artificial Intelligence: Agencies Have Begun Implementation but Need to Complete Key Requirements (GAO-24-105980)
measure: Completeness of 23 agencies' AI inventories and compliance with AI requirements
finding: 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI uses, but only 5 gave complete information for every use case.
limits: compliance audit; FY2022 round; not re-read this session

title: Where does federal AI spending stand in 2026?
measure: Federal contracts whose description mentions 'artificial intelligence' or 'AI': count, obligations and potential award value, by report period
latest_value: 1,743 contracts; $7.2bn obligated; $91.8bn potential value (Sep 2023–Mar 2026), up from $261m / $355m (2022 report) and $675m / $4.6bn (2024 report); Defense 98.9% of potential value
finding: Potential value of AI-labelled federal contracts rose from $355m to $4.6bn to $91.8bn across three report periods, almost all of it defence.
limits: keyword match on contract text; report periods of unequal length; potential value is a ceiling, not spending; vendor shares not in text read

title: GSA OneGov AI deals: some extensions, new offers
measure: Orders placed against GSA's government-wide AI offers and staff given access (count)
latest_value: More than 120 orders; about 3.4 million people across government with access (May 2026, GSA official)
finding: After OpenAI, Google and Anthropic offered models to agencies for about $0.47–$1 each, GSA reported over 120 orders giving about 3.4 million people access, with prices set to rise.
limits: access, not use; one official's figure via press; deals expiring Sep 2026

title: Anthropic, OpenAI and Palantir: who gains and who loses in the federal fallout
measure: Effects of the Pentagon's 2026 designation of Anthropic as a security risk on federal AI suppliers
finding: After Anthropic refused uses for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, the Pentagon dropped it and OpenAI became the default substitute, showing a state can switch frontier vendors quickly.
limits: analyst commentary; dates and legal scope not checked at primary source

title: DOGE builds AI tool to cut 50 percent of federal regulations
measure: Reported use of an AI tool to flag federal regulations for repeal
finding: Internal slides reportedly described an AI tool to review about 200,000 regulatory items with the aim of cutting half, claiming 93% less human review time.
limits: claims from leaked slides relayed second-hand; no count of rules actually rescinded; original Post article not read

title: Algorithmic transparency records
measure: Records published under the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (count)
latest_value: 152 records (12 Oct 2026; newest dated 9 Sep 2026)
finding: Official records rose from 6 (Oct 2023) to 152 (Oct 2026), mostly after the standard became mandatory for central government; an NGO had found 55 tools in Oct 2023.
limits: counts tools, not decisions; mandate-driven; includes non-AI algorithms

cite: Civil Service World 2026 (reporting Cabinet Office People Survey)
title: People Survey 2025: civil servants set out AI gains and expectations
measure: Share of civil servants saying using AI for work saves them at least an hour a week; share expecting AI to change their job within 5 years
latest_value: 27% save at least an hour a week; 76% expect AI to change their job (23 Sep–21 Oct 2025; 343,961 responses, 102 organisations)
finding: In the first People Survey to ask, 27% of 343,961 civil servants said AI saves them an hour or more a week, from 57% at DSIT to 6.5% at the Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service.
limits: one reading so far; time saved, not decisions; official results page not read

title: Microsoft 365 Copilot Experiment: Cross-Government Findings Report
measure: Self-reported time saved and adoption among 20,000 civil servants in 12 departments, Sep–Dec 2024
finding: Participants reported saving 26 minutes a day; 82% would not want to go back.
limits: self-report; 7,115 survey responses; not re-read this session

cite: Bright, Enock, Esnaashari et al. (Alan Turing Institute) 2024
title: Generative AI is already widespread in the public sector
measure: Share of 938 UK public-service professionals using generative AI, and with clear guidance
finding: 22% actively used generative AI while only 32% said there was clear guidance on its use.
limits: education, health, social work and emergency services, not core civil service; not re-read this session

title: Use of artificial intelligence in government
measure: Share of government bodies that had deployed or were piloting AI
finding: 37% of responding bodies had deployed AI, typically one or two use cases, and 70% were piloting or planning it.
limits: self-report snapshot; read via University of Exeter summary this session

title: Live Facial Recognition Annual Report 2025, and deployment records
measure: Live facial recognition deployments, faces scanned, AI alerts (true/false) and arrests per year
latest_value: 11 Sep 2024–10 Sep 2025: 203 hotspot deployments; about 3.15m faces; 2,077 alerts (10 false); 962 arrests. Deployments by calendar year: 4 (2020), 0 (2021), 5 (2022), 23 (2023), 180 (2024)
finding: London police use of AI face matching went from 5 deployments in 2022 to 180 in 2024; in the latest report year it raised 2,077 alerts, each reviewed by an officer, and led to 962 arrests.
limits: one force and one tool; calendar-year deployment counts compiled by London Assembly Greens from Met data; no figure for true alerts officers chose not to act on

cite: Observatory count, UK Parliament Hansard API 2026
title: Commons spoken contributions containing 'I rise to speak'
measure: House of Commons spoken contributions matching the phrase (count per period)
finding: A phrase typical of ChatGPT-drafted speeches jumped to 429 Commons contributions in the first half of 2025 (191–196 in each of 2022–23), then fell to 81 in the second half after press coverage in September 2025 and 82 in the first half of 2026.
limits: phrase proxy; 2024 election and new intake; drop after publicity may reflect editing rather than less AI use; press counts differ (231 for 2024)

title: UK government 'Consult' tool on live consultations
measure: AI analysis of public consultation responses: volume, agreement with human analysts
finding: Consult processed 50,000+ water-review responses in about 2 hours plus 22 hours of human checking, agreeing with human analysts 83% of the time.
limits: government's own evaluation via trade press; not re-read this session

title: Algoritmeregister dashboard
measure: Published algorithm descriptions by Dutch public bodies (count), by status and by category (A high-risk AI systems, B impactful, C other)
latest_value: 1,590 published (Oct 2026): 41 high-risk AI, 716 impactful, 833 other; 1,444 in use; 355 of 531 connected bodies publishing
finding: Published descriptions rose from 1,225 (Nov 2025) to 1,590 (Oct 2026); 'impactful' algorithms rose from 578 to 716, while high-risk AI systems stayed between 32 and 41.
limits: registration not mandatory for all bodies; includes rule-based algorithms; dashboard shows the last 12 months only; counts revised by about 1

title: Focus op AI bij de rijksoverheid
measure: AI systems reported by 70 central-government bodies; whether performance and risks are known
finding: 70 bodies reported 433 AI systems; for 35% of those in use they did not know whether the system worked as intended, and 5% appeared in the public register.
limits: read via secondary report; most systems classed 'minimal risk' by the bodies themselves; about two-thirds internal

title: DSA Transparency Database dashboard
measure: Statements of reasons for platform moderation decisions in a rolling 180 days, and share flagged as fully automated decisions
latest_value: 3,944,217,973 statements; 43% fully automated decisions; 373 platforms (dashboard read 12 Oct 2026, unchanged from 8 Oct)
finding: Platforms report about 3.9 billion moderation decisions in 180 days, 43% of them fully automated: the largest public per-decision count of automated decisions found.
limits: platform self-report; 'automated' is not always AI; dashboard gives no time series; figure unchanged across two reads

title: Automated Transparency: A Legal and Empirical Analysis of the Digital Services Act Transparency Database
measure: Automation flags and delays in 131 million statements of reasons, 19–28 Nov 2023
finding: Automation varies widely: X, LinkedIn and Booking.com report no automated decisions while AliExpress, Google Maps, Google Shopping and TikTok automate most or all.
limits: ten-day window; platform self-report; inconsistent fields

title: Trading nuance for scale? Platform observability and content governance under the DSA
measure: Automation, speed and territorial scope of 439 million statements of reasons from eight very large platforms
finding: The vast majority of moderation decisions were enforced automatically and uniformly across the EU, and automation correlated strongly with speed.
limits: abstract only read; no exact shares or trend

title: EU high-risk AI database delay; AI Act omnibus agreement
measure: Entries in the EU database of high-risk AI systems (count)
latest_value: 0: database not yet operational (Jul 2026); Annex III obligations deferred to 2 Dec 2027
finding: The EU's register of high-risk AI was not open in July 2026, and the obligations it supports were postponed by 16 months.
limits: secondary reports; not re-checked this session

title: Canada launches first register of AI uses in federal government
measure: AI systems listed by federal institutions (count)
latest_value: Over 400 systems from 42 institutions (launch, 28 Nov 2025); 409 when accessed 16 Dec 2025
finding: Canada's first federal AI register listed over 400 systems from 42 institutions at launch, with no fields on decisions or human review.
limits: one snapshot; no decision or oversight fields; update schedule not set

title: Bureaucratic Silences: What the Canadian AI Register Reveals, Omits, and Obscures (FAccT '26)
measure: Content analysis of 409 register entries: purpose, build source, vendors, data practices
finding: Of 409 systems, 86% serve staff rather than the public, 38% were built by vendors (Microsoft named in 46), and entries rarely say how humans review outputs.
limits: one snapshot; register self-report

title: Digital Government Outlook 2026, ch. 4: Adopting and governing AI in government (Digital Government Index 2025)
measure: Share of OECD countries reporting AI use in internal processes, public services, policymaking and oversight; share with guardrails
latest_value: 2025 (36 countries): internal processes 86%, public services 75%, policymaking 36%, oversight 33%; pre-deployment risk assessment 39%, post-deployment audits 31%, open algorithm register 17%
finding: Countries using AI in internal processes rose from 70% to 86% (2023–25) and in public services from 67% to 75%, but in policymaking only from 33% to 36%; under a third audit systems after deployment.
limits: country counts, not intensity; government self-report; sample changed 33 to 36; US and Germany missing in 2025

title: Government AI Readiness Index
measure: Composite readiness score of governments to use AI
latest_value: 2025 edition: 195 governments; US first
finding: Ranks capacity to adopt AI, not use, decisions or control; the 2025 method change breaks comparability.
limits: composite index; method break 2025; not re-read this session

cite: Public First for the Center for Data Innovation 2026
title: Public Sector AI Adoption Index 2026
measure: Share of public servants in 10 countries who use AI (survey, n = 3,335)
latest_value: Over 70% use AI; 18% say governments use AI effectively
finding: Over 70% of 3,335 public servants in 10 countries said they use AI, but only 18% said their government uses it effectively.
limits: sponsored by Google; opt-in panel; one wave; frequency not reported

title: Survey of generative AI use among state and local civil servants
measure: Share of state and local public employees in 12 states using generative AI for work
latest_value: About 25% use it; about 17% weekly (n > 1,000)
finding: One in four state and local civil servants in 12 states used generative AI for work and one in six weekly.
limits: one wave; fieldwork dates not given

title: Response to PQ on progress of adopting AI tools within public service
measure: Share of 150,000 public officers who have used the government chatbot; custom bots created
latest_value: About 80% have used Pair Chat; over 20,000 bots (Nov 2025)
finding: About four in five Singapore public officers had used the government chatbot by November 2025.
limits: 'have used' differs from other releases' 'users' and 'regularly use'; no vendor breakdown; not re-read this session

title: AI Hallucination Cases Database
measure: Court and tribunal decisions addressing AI-fabricated material in filings (cumulative count)
latest_value: 2,184 decisions (10 Oct 2026): US 1,492; Canada 233; Australia 112; UK 76; pro se 1,259; lawyers 864; judges 32
finding: Decisions catching AI-invented material reached 2,184 by 10 Oct 2026 (712 at end-2025 per Bloomberg Law); 32 involve judges.
limits: counts what judges catch and write up; rises with vigilance; latest months undercount

title: State of the Courts 2024: generative AI use
measure: Share of US state, county and municipal courts using or planning to use generative AI
latest_value: Under 10% using or planning to use within a year (early 2024)
finding: In early 2024, fewer than 10% of US state and local court respondents were using or planning to use generative AI tools.
limits: sample size not on page; later waves not found in this search

title: Federal judges report broad adoption of AI tools
measure: Share of responding US federal judges using at least one AI tool in judicial work
latest_value: 61.6% (Dec 2025; 112 of 502 sampled)
finding: 61.6% of responding federal judges used at least one AI tool, mostly for legal research; 5.4% daily.
limits: 22% response rate; on site already; not re-read this session

title: UNESCO survey uncovers critical gaps in AI training among judicial operators
measure: Share of judicial operators in 96 countries who had used AI tools for work, and had guidance
latest_value: 44% used AI tools; 9% had institutional guidance or training
finding: 44% of judicial operators had used AI tools such as ChatGPT for work while only 9% had institutional guidance.
limits: self-selected sample; not re-read this session

title: UAE Cabinet approves Regulatory Intelligence Office
measure: Formal assignment of AI to legislative drafting
finding: The UAE created an office to run 'AI-driven' lawmaking with a target of speeding it up by up to 70%.
limits: target, not result; no elected legislature; not re-read this session

title: Brazilian city enacts an ordinance secretly written by ChatGPT
measure: A law drafted by a chatbot
finding: A 36-member council unanimously passed an ordinance later revealed to be ChatGPT-drafted.
limits: single anecdote; not re-read this session

title: Albania's cheerful AI minister is the product of a government agency under investigation
measure: Formal ministerial title given to an AI system
finding: Albania named an AI system a minister of state in September 2025, but reporting says officials still make the decisions.
limits: symbolic; no evidence it decides tenders; not re-read this session

cite: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner 2026
title: Information Commissioner highlights transparency for agencies in automated decision-making
measure: Agencies authorised to use automated decision-making that disclose it (count)
finding: Only 4 of 23 Australian agencies authorised by law to use automated decision-making disclosed it; none listed decision counts.
limits: automation, not necessarily AI; not re-read this session

title: Automated decision-making systems in NSW public sector (executive report)
measure: Automated decision-making systems reported by NSW public bodies (count)
latest_value: 136 systems reported by 77 bodies (Mar 2024)
finding: NSW bodies reported 136 automated decision systems; the Ombudsman called it 'a mapping, not a counting', with no volumes or override rates.
limits: one-off; not re-read this session

title: Algorithmic Risk Assessment in the Hands of Humans
measure: Effect of a sentencing risk tool on Virginia judges' decisions
finding: Judges deviated from the tool's recommendations in systematic ways, so it had no detectable effect on reoffending.
limits: pre-generative tool; carried from landscape pass

title: Algorithmic Recommendations and Human Discretion
measure: Outcomes when bail judges override an algorithm's recommendation
finding: About 90% of judges did worse than the algorithm when they overrode it.
limits: pre-generative; carried from landscape pass

title: The Flaws of Policies Requiring Human Oversight of Government Algorithms
measure: Review of 41 policies requiring human oversight of government algorithms
finding: Policies assume people can oversee algorithms effectively; the evidence says they mostly cannot, so oversight should move to institutions.
limits: argument from review; carried from landscape pass

title: Putting a human in the loop: Increasing uptake, but decreasing accuracy of automated decision-making
measure: Uptake and accuracy when people may adjust an algorithm's output (n = 292)
finding: Letting people adjust the algorithm raised uptake by 7 points but made decisions slightly less accurate.
limits: lab task; on site in gap table

cite: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme 2023
title: Report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
measure: Harm from automated debt-raising without human review
finding: About 470,000 debts were wrongly raised by income averaging over 2016–2020, settled at A$1.872bn.
limits: rule-based automation, not AI; figures via earlier pass

title: 'Lavender': The AI machine directing Israel's bombing spree in Gaza
measure: Reported human review time per AI-nominated target
finding: Anonymous officers described about 20 seconds of human review per AI-nominated target; the Israeli military disputes the account.
limits: anonymous sources; contested

title: Algorithmic management in the workplace: new evidence from an OECD employer survey
measure: Share of firms using software to instruct, monitor or evaluate workers; managers reporting unclear accountability
latest_value: US 90%, European average 79%; 28% of managers report unclear accountability
finding: Most firms in six countries use algorithmic management, and 28% of managers say accountability for its decisions is unclear.
limits: very broad definition; figures via union summary; not re-read this session

title: Gartner predicts at least 80% of governments will deploy AI agents to automate routine decision-making by 2028
measure: Share of governments deploying AI agents for routine decisions (2028); share of agencies requiring explainability and human-in-the-loop (2029)
finding: Forecasts at least 80% of governments using AI agents for routine decisions by 2028, and 70% of agencies requiring human-in-the-loop for citizen-facing automated decisions by 2029.
limits: vendor-analyst forecast; method not stated; 'deploy' undefined

title: Abu Dhabi aims to be world's first fully AI-native government by 2027
measure: Stated target: 100% process automation across digital services by 2027
finding: Target of a fully 'AI-native' government by 2027 with 100% process automation and AED 13bn of spending.
limits: a goal, not a forecast with a method; no progress audit found

title: A Formal Model of How Artificial Intelligence Erodes Human Agency (RR-A4817-1)
measure: Proposed metrics: distribution of decisive coalitions, minimal decisive coalition size, and its human/AI composition
finding: A social-choice model shows agency can erode through human disenfranchisement, AI enfranchisement and AI agenda control even when AI is aligned; it recommends tracking coalition composition over time and benchmarking reversibility.
limits: theory; metrics not yet applied to real institutions

title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development
measure: Proposed state metrics such as the fraction of decisions made by AI and AI's role in law and policymaking
finding: Names the share of state decisions made by AI and AI's role in legal and policy processes as metrics to monitor.
limits: framework; no data

title: M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
measure: Defines 'high-impact AI' and minimum practices (testing, impact assessment, human oversight, appeals) agencies must report
finding: High-impact AI is AI whose output is a principal basis for decisions with legal, material or significant effects; agencies must apply minimum practices or stop using it, with waivers allowed.
limits: requires reporting of safeguards, not of decision volumes or overrides; wording via earlier pass and the inventory data dictionary

title: DSA statement-of-reasons schema (automated detection / automated decision flags)
measure: Per-decision flags for fully, partly or not automated decisions
finding: The only per-decision automation flag in force found in this search; a template for counting automated state decisions.
limits: applies to platforms, not governments
